categories.reason: The premise of a journalist investigating a suspicious drowning is engaging and sets up a classic whodunit scenario.
The opening hook effectively establishes the scene and introduces the victim, Dr. Mallory Finch, creating immediate intrigue.
The plot structure is coherent but somewhat convoluted, with multiple characters and timelines that could confuse readers.
Character clarity is generally good, but some characters, particularly Sylvia and Beatrice, could use more depth to distinguish their motivations.
Dialogue is mostly natural and serves to reveal character dynamics, though some exchanges feel overly expository.
The atmosphere is well-crafted, with vivid descriptions of the seaside setting that enhance the mood of mystery and tension.
Clues are present but not always planted effectively; the tide chart is introduced early but its significance is not fully realized until later.
Pacing is uneven; some sections drag with excessive detail while others rush through critical moments, particularly in the climax.
The ending provides a resolution to the mystery, but the emotional impact is somewhat muted by the preceding exposition.
Prose is generally readable, but there are moments of awkward phrasing and overly complex sentences that detract from clarity.
